move.title: A crisp crust under a soft custard
move.body: A quiche is a savory pie: a butter crust filled with eggs, cream, cheese, and vegetables. Today you'll make the pastry, bake it empty first so the bottom stays crisp, cook the spinach and mushrooms dry, and bake the custard gently until it's just set.

why.title: Cold butter, flaky crust
why.body: Pieces of cold butter coated in flour melt in the oven and leave flaky pockets. Butter that warms and smears in makes the crust tough or greasy.

why.title: Just enough water
why.body: Water lets flour build gluten. Pastry wants only enough to hold together when squeezed; more makes it tough, and it shrinks in the oven.

why.title: Why bake the crust first
why.body: A wet custard poured into raw pastry soaks it before it can bake, and the bottom comes out pale and soggy. Baking the crust empty first, weighted so it keeps its shape, sets it crisp.

why.title: Cook the water out
why.body: Mushrooms and spinach are mostly water. Cooked first until the pan is dry, they won't weep into the custard and make it runny.

why.title: Gentle heat for custard
why.body: Eggs set smooth at a low oven temperature. Too hot, and the custard puffs, cracks, and turns watery. It's done when the middle still jiggles a little; it finishes setting as it cools.

wrong.sign: The crust shrank down the sides
wrong.fix: The dough was stretched into the plate or not chilled. Ease it in loosely, and chill it before baking.
The crust wasn't baked long enough before filling. Bake it until it looks dry and light golden.
The vegetables weren't cooked dry, or it baked too hot. Cook them until the pan is dry next time.
It baked too long or too hot. Take it out while the center still jiggles.

quiz.q: Why bake the crust before filling it?
choices: So the bottom sets crisp before the wet custard goes in

quiz.q: Why cook the spinach and mushrooms first?
choices: To cook out their water so the custard isn't runny
The edges are set and the center jiggles a little
The center is firm and puffed
The top is brown and cracked
quiz.explain: It finishes setting as it cools.

steps.text: Spread the butter cubes on the plate and put them in the freezer. Put the water in a cup with a few ice cubes.
Whisk the crust's flour and salt in the large bowl. Add the cold butter and press it in with the back of the fork until the biggest pieces are the size of peas.
steps.look: Coarse crumbs, with pea-sized bits of butter.

steps.text: Sprinkle 3 tablespoons of the ice water over it, leaving the ice behind, and toss with the fork. Squeeze a handful. If it crumbles, add more water a tablespoon at a time.
steps.look: Shaggy, but a squeezed handful holds together.

steps.text: Press the dough into a flat disk, cover it, and chill it.
Put a rack in the lower third of the oven, set the sheet pan on it, and heat the oven to 400°F.

Roll the dough on a floured counter into a 12-inch circle, about ⅛ inch thick. Ease it into the pie plate without stretching it. Trim the edge to ½ inch past the rim, fold it under, and press it with the fork.
steps.tip: Roll from the middle out, turning the dough a quarter turn each time.

steps.text: Put the crust in the freezer to firm up.
Line the crust with foil and fill it with the pie weights. Bake it on the hot sheet pan.
With oven mitts, take out the pan. Lift out the foil and weights, and bake the crust until the bottom looks dry and light golden.
steps.look: Dry and light golden, with no shiny raw spots.

steps.text: While the crust bakes, slice the mushrooms. Cook them in the tablespoon of butter in the skillet over medium-high heat until browned and the pan is dry. Add the spinach and stir until it wilts.
steps.look: Browned mushrooms, wilted spinach, and no liquid in the pan.

steps.text: Spread the vegetables on the plate to cool. Turn the oven down to 350°F.
Whisk the eggs, cream, milk, the filling's salt, and the pepper in the medium bowl.
steps.look: Smooth and pale yellow, with no streaks of white.

steps.text: Wash your hands with soap, and throw away the eggshells.
Scatter the cheese and the vegetables in the crust. Pour the custard over them slowly.
steps.tip: Pull the rack out partway and fill it in the oven if it's easier than carrying it full.

steps.text: Bake until the edges are set and the center still jiggles a little.
steps.look: Puffed and set at the edges, a gentle wobble in the middle.

steps.text: With oven mitts, pull out the rack. Push the butter knife in 1 inch from the center. It should come out clean. If not, bake 5 more minutes.

target.look: A knife 1 inch from the center comes out clean

steps.text: Turn off the oven. Let the quiche cool on the rack before slicing.
steps.tip: It finishes setting as it cools.

freeze-butter.text: Cube the butter, spread it on the plate, and freeze it. Put the water in a cup with ice.

cut-in.text: Weigh 6 ounces of flour into the large bowl and whisk in the crust's salt. Cut in the butter with the fork to pea size.
cut-in.look: Coarse crumbs, with pea-sized bits of butter.

water.text: Toss in ice water a tablespoon at a time, usually 3 to 4, until a squeezed handful just holds.

chill.text: Press into a disk, wrap, and chill.
chill.tip: The dough keeps 2 days in the fridge, so it can be made ahead.

oven.text: Set the sheet pan on a rack in the lower third and heat the oven to 400°F.

roll.text: Roll a 12-inch round ⅛ inch thick. Ease it into the pie plate, trim to ½ inch past the rim, fold under, and flute the edge with your fingers.

blind.text: Line with foil, fill with the weights, and bake on the hot pan.

unweight.text: Lift out the foil and weights. Bake until the bottom is dry and golden, not just pale.
unweight.look: Golden all over, with no shiny or translucent spots.

wash-egg.text: Wash your hands, and throw away the shells.

veg.text: Slice the mushrooms ¼ inch thick. Brown them in the filling's butter over medium-high heat until the pan is dry, then wilt in the spinach.

custard.text: Whisk the cream, milk, salt, and pepper into the eggs.

fill.text: Scatter the cheese and vegetables in the crust, set it on the pan in the oven, and pour in the custard.

bake.text: Bake until the edges are set and the center wobbles slightly.

check.text: Check the center with the thermometer: 170°F. Under, bake 5 minutes more.

cool.text: Cool on the rack before slicing.

add.text: Meanwhile, beat the eggs in the medium bowl.
Brush the hot crust with 1 tablespoon of the beaten egg and bake 2 more minutes. Turn the oven down to 325°F.
add.look: A dry, matte coat on the bottom.

add.text: Tip the vegetables onto the towel, let them cool a few minutes, then wring out the liquid.

move.title: Blind-baked, sealed, set at 170°F
move.body: A quiche fails at the bottom: a pale, wet crust under the custard. You'll weigh and blind-bake the crust until it's golden, seal it with egg, wring the vegetables dry, and bake the custard low until the center reads 170°F.

wrong.sign: The crust shrank down the sides
wrong.fix: The dough was stretched into the plate or not chilled. Ease it in loosely, and chill it before baking.
The crust wasn't baked long enough before filling. Bake it until it looks dry and light golden.
The vegetables weren't cooked dry, or it baked too hot. Cook them until the pan is dry next time.
It baked too long or too hot. Take it out while the center still jiggles.

wrong.sign: The custard curdled at the edges
wrong.fix: The oven ran hot or it baked too long. Pull it at 170°F next time, and check your oven with a thermometer.

quiz.q: What does brushing the hot crust with egg do?
choices: Seals it so the custard can't soak in
quiz.explain: It cooks into a thin layer.

quiz.q: What temperature is the center of the custard done at?
quiz.explain: It firms more as it cools.

quiz.q: Why squeeze the cooked spinach in a towel?
choices: To get the last water out before it hits the custard

quiz.q: Why bake the custard at 325°F, not 400°F?
choices: So the edges don't overcook while the center sets

add.title: An egg seal
add.body: A thin coat of beaten egg brushed on the hot crust cooks in 2 minutes into a waterproof layer between pastry and custard.

add.title: 170°F, low and slow
add.body: Custard sets between 165 and 180°F. At 325°F the outside doesn't overshoot while the center catches up. At 170°F in the middle it's set but still silky; it firms more as it cools.
